title: Stars and Constellations
lead: The Bible names a few star groups (the Pleiades, Orion and the Bear), praises God who made the stars and counts them, and forbids worshiping them or reading the future in them. This page is about the stars as part of the natural world. The worship of the sun, moon and stars has its own page (The Host of Heaven), and so does the star the magi followed (The Magi).

sections.b: In Genesis 1 the stars come almost as an afterthought: God made the two big lights "and the stars" (Genesis 1:16). Gerhard Hasel points out that the chapter does not even name the sun and moon, whose common names were also the names of gods, and gives them the humble job of lights that "govern" day and night; he reads this as a quiet protest against star worship. God "counts how many stars there are; / he calls each of them by a name" (Psalm 147:4; compare Isaiah 40:26). Abraham is told, "Look toward the sky and number the stars, if you can number them" (Genesis 15:5), and Jeremiah says "the army of the heavens cannot be counted" (Jeremiah 33:22). God "has fixed the rules for the moon and stars to light the night" (Jeremiah 31:35). In poetry the stars sing at creation (Job 38:7) and fight for Israel: "The stars fought from heaven" (Judges 5:20).

sections.b:
Three star groups are named, always as God's work: "The Bear is his work, and Orion, and the Pleiades" (Job 9:9; compare Job 38:31–32; Amos 5:8). The Hebrew names are kimah (most likely the Pleiades), kesil (Orion; the word also means "fool") and 'ash or 'ayish (the Bear, though this one is least certain). The plural kesilim, "Orions," means the constellations in general (Isaiah 13:10). The old translators were not sure either: the Greek of Job 9:9 has "the Pleiades and Hesperus and Arcturus," and the Greek of Amos 5:8 names no stars at all. The KJV's "Arcturus with his sons" follows that tradition.

God asks Job, "Can you tie the knots that hold the Pleiades, / or untie the ropes of Orion?" (Job 38:31). The KJV's "sweet influences of Pleiades" takes the rare word ma'adannot as "delights"; most now read "bonds" or "knots," which fits the parallel "ropes." The next verse asks about the mazzarot (Job 38:32), found only here; the Greek just copies it as Mazouroth, and the KJV as "Mazzaroth." It is probably close to the mazzalot, the "star signs" that Josiah stopped people from worshiping (2 Kings 23:5). In later Hebrew mazzal means a constellation, the word the Talmud uses below.

The lights of the sky are "signs" for times and seasons (Genesis 1:14), but Israel was not to bow to them (Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3) or fear them: "Do not panic at the signs in the sky, / though the nations panic at them" (Jeremiah 10:2). Isaiah mocks Babylon's experts, "the ones who map out the sky, / who stare at the stars" (Isaiah 47:13), who cannot save her. The magi of Matthew 2 did read a star, and Matthew tells it as God leading the nations to the newborn king (Matthew 2:2; Matthew 2:9–10); what the star was is discussed under The Magi.

Jewish views. The Talmud records a debate. Rabbi Yochanan taught, "There is no constellation for the Jewish people," citing Jeremiah 10:2, and tells how God led Abraham outside and told him to leave his star charts behind (compare Genesis 15:5). Rabbi Chanina held that "there is a constellation for the Jewish people" (Shabbat 156a).

Christian views. Augustine had once trusted astrologers. In his Confessions (7.6) he tells how a friend's father and a slave's child were born at the same moment under the same stars but lived very different lives, and how twins such as Esau and Jacob show the same thing; whatever the astrologers got right, he concluded, came "not by art, but by chance." The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2116) rejects "consulting horoscopes, astrology" along with other divination. Astronomy, the study of the stars, is another matter: Calvin praised it as a study "not to be reprobated."
